description: ¡Hola! Somos Allinkay (quechua para "estar bien"). Un equipo multidisciplinario con base en ingeniería (Civil, Mecatrónica, Informática y UX/UI), unidos por la curiosidad de explorar y aprender en la NASA Space Apps. Desarrollamos software de salud para astronautas. Buscamos mentes apasionadas por la tecnología y, especialmente, perfiles de Bioingeniería, Biomedicina o Ciencias de la Salud para interpretar datos fisiológicos. ¡Ven a explorar con nosotros!
summary:
ALLINKAY is an onboard health monitor for astronauts that works without waiting for Earth. On a Mars mission, help from Earth arrives up to 22 minutes late, and health data is still compared with general reference ranges that hide personal changes: in NASA's open Inspiration4 data, three of four crew members had 14% to 27% fewer white blood cells after landing, yet never left the general range.

ALLINKAY compares every signal with each astronaut's own normal: sleep, reaction time, mood, white blood cells, glucose, oxygen, cabin air and radiation. It alerts only when a change is confirmed, explains why it matters with its NASA source, and says what to do. It spots combined patterns, forecasts sleep three nights ahead and tracks radiation up to NASA's 600 mSv career limit. The demo uses real NASA data for the commander's blood baselines, the ISS cabin and the radiation Curiosity measured on its way to Mars. We also measured false alarms: about one every 12 astronaut-years, with 99.6% of simulated changes detected within 10 days.
details:
What it does. ALLINKAY is decision support that lives on the spacecraft. It has one screen, "Mission Health":

·         In the center, a 3D hologram of the astronaut's body (skin, skeleton, brain, heart and airways, adapted from the BodyParts3D anatomy atlas), with a bubble for each system: neurological, cardiovascular, immune, radiation, ship environment and the personal model. A line joins each bubble to the part of the body it watches, and only what needs attention turns amber or red. In the field, the hologram wears NASA's Z2 spacesuit, its prototype for planetary surfaces, with the brain and heart still visible inside.

·         On the left, who is being watched, their overall state, and the cognitive tests our biomedical engineer is building (reaction time, memory, patterns and spatial orientation), shown as in development.

·         On the right, the latest trends, the model's reading of confirmed changes, and the actions: an emergency guide and the routine to mitigate each change.

The demo follows a crew of three on a Mars mission: a commander and a mission scientist in the ship, and a flight engineer working outside. Over ten mission days, the commander's sleep, reaction time, mood and white blood cells drift, and the screen first raises an early warning, then a combined pattern. The radiation dose is not simulated: it replays what Curiosity's RAD measured on its way to Mars in March 2012 (NASA PDS), and when the solar storm's second wave crosses ten times the usual rate, the emergency guide opens for the whole crew and names the real storm from NASA's DONKI catalogue. The commander's white blood cell and glucose normals come from Inspiration4 (NASA OSDR, OSD-569 and OSD-575) and the cabin is centred on the real ISS cabin (NASA OSDR EDA); every other reading is synthetic.

How it works. Each signal is compared with the person's own baseline from before flight, not with a general range. To keep false alarms down without missing real changes:

·         Personal normals are judged with a prediction interval, because they come from a limited reference period.

·         Live signals must stay outside the normal for 10 readings in a row, and daily signals on 3 of the last 4 days.

·         An unusual lab exam is repeated the next day and alerts only if the repeat agrees, with the 99.5% reference change value built on the EFLM within-subject variation.

·         Combined patterns: when two or more systems change at once, the alert says so.

·         Sleep forecast: the next three nights are projected with Holt's exponential smoothing and an 80% band.

·         Radiation: a ledger integrates the dose rate; ten times the usual rate is a solar storm, and NASA's 600 mSv career limit raises an emergency.

·         Spacewalks: in field mode only the portable sensors are watched: heart rate, oxygen, body temperature and dose.

Validity. No monitor can have zero false alarms and zero missed changes, so we measured both with a script that runs the same loop as the app, on 200 synthetic people over 90 days: in the ship, 5 false alarms in 60 astronaut-years (about one every 12 years); in the field, none; and 1195 of 1200 scripted changes detected within 10 days. The model must be validated on real data before it is used with people.

Benefits and impact. The crew sees problems early, even inside the general ranges, without waiting for Earth. Alerts are explained, cite their NASA source and say what to do, so they can be trusted and acted on. It scales to a whole crew, each person with their own normal, and it works fully offline, as it would on board.

What makes it creative. Instead of asking "is this value normal for people?", ALLINKAY asks "is this normal for this astronaut?", and shows the answer on the body itself, as a hologram the whole crew can read at a glance. Real NASA measurements drive the story: Inspiration4 blood tests, the ISS cabin, and the radiation storm Curiosity lived through on its way to Mars.

Factors we considered: the communication delay and blackouts (everything runs on board); the balance between false alarms and missed changes, which we measured instead of assuming; NASA's radiation limits (NASA-STD-3001); privacy (no real person's data in the repository, and test results stay on the device); and that it is decision support, not a diagnosis.

Next steps. Real sensors: our biomedical engineer already made a first bench recording with an AD8232 ECG module, and the hardware roadmap plans an ESP32 sensor hub with an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano as the onboard computer. Then validation with real astronaut data, and a link to Earth that integrates delayed feedback. The cabin system could also watch air quality (volatile organic compounds, carbon monoxide and microbes), as NASA's DSO 611 experiment measured on the Space Shuttle.

Tools.

·         Backend: Python 3.13, FastAPI, Pydantic, NumPy, SQLite and Uvicorn.

·         Frontend: React 19, Vite, TypeScript and three.js (the 3D hologram).

·         Quality: Ruff, pytest, ESLint, Vitest and gitleaks, run by GitHub Actions on every pull request.

Deployment: Docker on Render. Open source under the Apache 2.0 licence.
